blocks.html: A symmetry group $G$ must act on the Hilbert space $\mathcal H$ in a way that respects superposition (linear) and probabilities (scalar product): by unitary operators $U(g)$ that compose like the group elements.

Invariant subspace. $K\subset\mathcal H$ with $U(g)K\subset K$ for every $g$: the symmetry never leads out of $K$. The representation is irreducible if the only invariant subspaces are $\{0\}$ and $\mathcal H$, otherwise reducible.

blocks.label: script Ch. 7.3: unitarity makes the complement invariant

blocks.html: So a unitary representation splits, $\mathcal H=K\oplus K^\perp$, with block diagonal $U(g)$; repeating gives a direct sum of irreducibles. For a compact group like SO(3) or SU(2) every finite-dimensional representation can be made unitary (average a scalar product over the group), and every irreducible one is finite-dimensional.

Which irreducibles exist? Through $U(R(\vec e,\theta))=e^{-i\theta\,\vec e\cdot\vec M}$ each representation gives generators with $[M_j,M_k]=i\varepsilon_{jkl}M_l$. In an irreducible one, the ladder from the top state $M_+\psi_j=0$ spans everything:

blocks.label: script Ch. 7.4: the irreducible representation $\mathcal D_j$, $\dim=2j+1$

blocks.html: Irreducible representations are the prime numbers of the theory. Rotations mix the states $|j,m\rangle$ with the same $j$ among themselves but never mix different $j$: that is why $j$ is a good quantum number of every rotation-invariant Hamiltonian, and why each energy level of such an $H$ carries a whole $(2j+1)$-plet.

Complete reducibility needs unitarity. $(\mathbb R,+)$ acting on $\mathbb C^2$ by $U(t)=\begin{pmatrix}1&t\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ is a representation with the invariant line $\mathrm{span}(e_1)$ but no invariant complement. Also: irreducible means no subspace is invariant under all $g$ at once; each single rotation does preserve its own axis.
Typical tasks: show $K^\perp$ is invariant (the one line above); state why $j$ labels the irreducibles; decompose a given representation (dimension count, $m$ multiplicities).

check.q: Which property of $U(g)$ is used to show that $K^\perp$ is invariant when $K$ is?
check.explain: $\langle\chi|U(g)\psi\rangle=\langle U(g^{-1})\chi|\psi\rangle$ and $U(g^{-1})\chi\in K$. Unitary operators preserve orthogonality.
$m$ runs from $-j$ to $j$ in integer steps.

check.q: SO(3) acting on $\mathbb R^4$ by $D(R)=\begin{pmatrix}R&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ is
options: reducible: $\mathbb R^3\oplus\mathbb R$, i.e. $\mathcal D_1\oplus\mathcal D_0$
check.explain: The first three coordinates rotate among themselves, the fourth is left alone: two invariant subspaces.

blocks.html: Package a vector as a traceless hermitian matrix and let $g\in\mathrm{SU}(2)$ act by conjugation:

blocks.tex: \tilde x=x^j\sigma_j=\begin{pmatrix}x^3&x^1-ix^2\\x^1+ix^2&-x^3\end{pmatrix},\quad \det\tilde x=-\vec x\cdot\vec x,\quad \tilde x\mapsto g\tilde xg^\dagger
blocks.label: script Ch. 7.5

blocks.html: $g\tilde xg^\dagger$ is again traceless hermitian with the same determinant, so it is a length-preserving linear map $R(g)$ of $\mathbb R^3$, in SO(3) because SU(2) is connected. $g$ and $-g$ give the same rotation and nothing else does: the kernel is $\{\pm\mathbb 1\}$ and

In $\mathcal D_j$ the rotation by $2\pi$ is $e^{-2\pi iM_3}=(-1)^{2j}\mathbb 1$. Integer $j$: honest representations of SO(3). Half-integer $j$: honest representations of SU(2) only; for SO(3) they hold up to a sign.
Projective representations (7.6). States are rays, so a symmetry only has to compose up to a phase. Associativity of the operator product forces the cocycle condition:

Re-phasing $\hat U(g)=c(g)U(g)$ of an honest representation gives the trivial cocycle $c(g,h)=\frac{c(g)c(h)}{c(gh)}$ (a coboundary), which can be removed again. A genuine cocycle cannot. Then the projective representation is an honest one of a covering group: for SO(3) the phases are $\pm1$ and the cover is SU(2).

Spin of the electron (7.7). $\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R^3)\otimes\mathbb C^2$, rotations act on both factors, $U(R)=U_{\rm orb}(R)\otimes e^{-i\theta\,\vec e\cdot\vec\sigma/2}$, generated by $\vec J=\vec L+\vec S$, $\vec S=\frac\hbar2\vec\sigma$.
One turn around a closed loop in SO(3) lifts to half a turn in SU(2), ending at $-\mathbb 1$; only a $4\pi$ turn closes. The sign is invisible in any probability, so physics allows it.

Half-integer $j$ never appear in orbital angular momentum: $Y_{lm}\propto e^{im\varphi}$ must be single-valued as a function on the sphere, so $m$ and hence $l$ are integers. Spin is not a function on the sphere; that is how $j=\frac12$ gets in.
Sheet 10 Q2 is the finite toy model: $\mathbb Z_2\times\mathbb Z_2$ with $\gamma(g)\gamma(h)=-\gamma(h)\gamma(g)$; the cocycle is genuine and the cover is $D_4$.

check.q: What is the kernel of $\mathrm{SU}(2)\to\mathrm{SO}(3)$, $g\mapsto R(g)$?
check.explain: $g\tilde xg^\dagger=\tilde x$ for all $\vec x$ means $g$ commutes with all $\sigma_j$, so $g=\lambda\mathbb 1$ with $\det g=\lambda^2=1$.

check.q: When can the cocycle of a projective representation be removed by re-phasing $U(g)\to c(g)U(g)$?
check.explain: That is a coboundary. For an abelian group with anticommuting images (sheet 10 Q2) it cannot be removed.

source.where: lecturer chapter 7 reading pack (HS26), explainer (served by the game server, not in git)

blocks.html: What must a symmetry preserve? Only what can be measured: the transition probabilities between rays,

Wigner’s theorem. A bijection of the rays that preserves all $P(\phi,\psi)$ is induced by an operator $U$ that is either unitary (linear, $\langle U\phi|U\psi\rangle=\langle\phi|\psi\rangle$) or anti-unitary; $U$ is unique up to a phase, which is where the cocycle of 7.6 comes from.

Weyl’s lemma. $U(g)^2$ is always unitary (two conjugations cancel), so $U(g^2)=c(g,g)^{-1}U(g)^2$ is unitary. Every rotation is a square, $R(\vec e,\varphi)=R(\vec e,\varphi/2)^2$, so rotations (and every element of a connected group) act unitarily. Anti-unitary operators are left for discrete symmetries that reverse time.
Time reversal. $\Psi(-t,\vec x)$ solves $i\partial_t\Psi=-H\Psi$: the wrong sign, since the equation is first order in $t$. Complex conjugation repairs it for a real $H$:

blocks.tex: (\mathcal T\Psi)(t,\vec x)=\overline{\Psi(-t,\vec x)},\qquad \vec x\to\vec x,\quad \vec p\to-\vec p,\quad \vec L\to-\vec L
blocks.label: anti-unitary

blocks.html: Running the film backwards: positions stay, velocities and angular momenta flip. A plane wave $e^{ikx}$ becomes $e^{-ikx}$. Bound states of a real $H$ can be chosen real, i.e. $\mathcal T$-invariant.

An anti-unitary symmetry has no hermitian generator ($e^{-i\theta T}$ makes no sense), so time-reversal invariance gives no conserved quantity, only selection rules. For spin $\frac12$, $\mathcal T=-i\sigma_2K$ with $\mathcal T^2=-\mathbb 1$: every level of an odd-electron system without magnetic field is at least doubly degenerate (Kramers).
Know the statement (unitary or anti-unitary), why rotations are unitary (squares), and the time-reversal example with its action on $\vec x,\vec p,\vec L$.

check.q: Why must every rotation be represented by a unitary (not anti-unitary) operator?
options: Every rotation is the square of another rotation, and the square of an anti-unitary operator is unitary
Rotations are continuous functions of the angle

check.explain: $\vec x$ stays, $\vec p\to-\vec p$, so $\vec x\wedge\vec p\to-\vec x\wedge\vec p$.
It is the conjugate scalar product: same modulus, so probabilities are preserved.

enc.title: Unitary representations are completely reducible

source.where: Ch. 7.3; lecturer ch7 pack: Reducible and irreducible representations

enc.goal: Show that for a unitary representation an invariant subspace $K$ has an invariant complement, so $\mathcal H$ splits into irreducibles; show where unitarity is essential.

steps.reveal: $\langle\chi|U(g)\psi\rangle=\langle U(g)^\dagger\chi|\psi\rangle=\langle U(g^{-1})\chi|\psi\rangle=0$, since $U(g^{-1})\chi\in K$ ($g^{-1}\in G$, $K$ invariant) and $\psi\perp K$.

steps.prompt: What does this mean for the matrices $U(g)$ in a basis adapted to $K\oplus K^\perp$?
steps.reveal: Both blocks are invariant, so every $U(g)=\begin{pmatrix}U_K(g)&0\\0&U_{K^\perp}(g)\end{pmatrix}$: two smaller representations.

steps.prompt: Why does repeating this end in irreducibles (finite dimension)?
steps.reveal: Each step strictly lowers the dimension of the pieces; when no piece has a non-trivial invariant subspace, all are irreducible: $\mathcal H=\mathcal H_1\oplus\mathcal H_2\oplus\dots$

steps.prompt: Show that unitarity is essential with $(\mathbb R,+)$ on $\mathbb C^2$, $U(t)=\begin{pmatrix}1&t\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$.
steps.reveal: $U(t)U(s)=U(t+s)$: a representation. $\mathrm{span}(e_1)$ is invariant. A complement would be a line spanned by $(a,1)$ with $U(t)(a,1)=(a+t,1)$, not on the line for $t\neq0$: no invariant complement. $U(t)$ is not unitary.

steps.prompt: Why may one assume unitarity for SO(3) anyway?
steps.reveal: Compact group: average any scalar product, $\langle v,w\rangle_{\rm inv}=\int\langle D(R)v,D(R)w\rangle\,dR$; by invariance of the Haar measure all $D(S)$ are unitary for it.

enc.title: $\mathrm{SU}(2)\to\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is a double cover

source.where: Ch. 7.5; lecturer ch7 pack: SO(3) versus SU(2)

enc.goal: With $\tilde x=x^j\sigma_j$ show that $\tilde x\mapsto g\tilde xg^\dagger$ defines a rotation $R(g)\in\mathrm{SO}(3)$, that the kernel is $\{\pm\mathbb 1\}$, and that $\varphi=2\pi$ lifts to $-\mathbb 1$.

steps.prompt: Show $\tilde x$ is traceless hermitian, recover $\vec x$ from it and compute $\det\tilde x$.
steps.reveal: Real combination of hermitian traceless matrices. $x^j=\frac12\mathrm{tr}(\tilde x\sigma_j)$. $\det\tilde x=-(x^3)^2-(x^1-ix^2)(x^1+ix^2)=-\vec x\cdot\vec x$.

steps.prompt: Show $g\tilde xg^\dagger$ is again some $\tilde x^\prime$ and $|\vec x^\prime|=|\vec x|$.
steps.reveal: $(g\tilde xg^\dagger)^\dagger=g\tilde xg^\dagger$, $\mathrm{tr}(g\tilde xg^\dagger)=\mathrm{tr}\tilde x=0$; linear in $\vec x$. $\det(g\tilde xg^\dagger)=\det\tilde x$, so lengths are preserved: $R(g)\in\mathrm O(3)$.

steps.prompt: Why $\det R(g)=+1$, and why is $g\mapsto R(g)$ a homomorphism?
steps.reveal: $R(g_1g_2)$: $g_1g_2\tilde x(g_1g_2)^\dagger=g_1(g_2\tilde xg_2^\dagger)g_1^\dagger$, so $R(g_1g_2)=R(g_1)R(g_2)$. SU(2) is connected and $R(\mathbb 1)=\mathbb 1$; $\det R$ is continuous with values $\pm1$, hence $+1$.

$g\tilde xg^\dagger=\tilde x$ for all $\vec x$ $\Leftrightarrow$ $g\sigma_j=\sigma_jg$ for all $j$ $\Rightarrow$ $g=\lambda\mathbb 1$ (Schur, or by hand), and $\det g=\lambda^2=1$: $g=\pm\mathbb 1$. So two elements of SU(2) sit above every rotation.

steps.prompt: Compute the rotation of $g=e^{-i\varphi\sigma_3/2}$ and its value at $\varphi=2\pi$.
steps.reveal: $g=\mathrm{diag}(e^{-i\varphi/2},e^{i\varphi/2})$ gives $x^1+ix^2\mapsto e^{i\varphi}(x^1+ix^2)$: $R(\vec e_3,\varphi)$. At $\varphi=2\pi$, $R=\mathbb 1$ but $g=-\mathbb 1$; $g$ returns to $\mathbb 1$ only at $4\pi$.

enc.title: Weyl's lemma: rotations act unitarily

source.where: Ch. 7.8; lecturer ch7 pack: Wigner's theorem and Weyl's lemma

enc.goal: Given Wigner (each $U(g)$ unitary or anti-unitary, $U(g)U(h)=c(g,h)U(gh)$), show that every rotation is represented unitarily.

steps.prompt: Show that $U^2$ is unitary if $U$ is anti-unitary.
steps.reveal: $U^2$ is linear (two conjugations) and $\langle U^2\phi|U^2\psi\rangle=\overline{\langle U\phi|U\psi\rangle}=\langle\phi|\psi\rangle$. If $U$ is unitary, $U^2$ trivially is.
$U(g)^2=c(g,g)U(g^2)$, so $U(g^2)=c(g,g)^{-1}U(g)^2$: a phase times a unitary operator, hence unitary.

steps.prompt: Why is every rotation a square?
steps.reveal: Same axis: generators commute, $e^{\alpha\Omega(\vec e)}e^{\beta\Omega(\vec e)}=e^{(\alpha+\beta)\Omega(\vec e)}$, so $R(\vec e,\varphi)=R(\vec e,\varphi/2)^2$. Hence $U(R)$ is unitary for every $R$.

steps.prompt: Which symmetries can then be anti-unitary at all?
steps.reveal: Only elements that are not squares: in practice the discrete ones that reverse time (time reversal $\mathcal T=K$ on wave functions). For a connected group (rotations, translations) everything is unitary, and Stone’s theorem gives hermitian generators.

enc.title: Time reversal is anti-unitary; Kramers degeneracy

source.where: Ch. 7.8; lecturer ch7 pack: Time reversal

enc.goal: Find the time-reversal operator for $i\hbar\partial_t\Psi=H\Psi$ with real $H$, its action on $\vec x,\vec p,\vec L$, and show $\mathcal T^2=-\mathbb 1$ forces double degeneracy for spin $\frac12$.

steps.prompt: Try $\Phi(t)=\Psi(-t)$. Which equation does it solve?
steps.reveal: $i\hbar\partial_t\Phi=-H\Phi$: the wrong sign, because the Schrödinger equation is first order in $t$.
$\partial_t\Phi=-\overline{(\partial_t\Psi)(-t)}=-\overline{\tfrac1{i\hbar}H\Psi(-t)}=\tfrac1{i\hbar}H\Phi$ for real $H$: a solution. At fixed $t$ this is complex conjugation $K$, anti-unitary.
$K\vec xK=\vec x$, $K(-i\hbar\nabla)K=+i\hbar\nabla=-\vec p$, so $\vec L\to-\vec L$; spin must flip too, $\mathcal T\vec\sigma\mathcal T^{-1}=-\vec\sigma$ with $\mathcal T=-i\sigma_2K$.

Anti-unitarity: $\langle\mathcal T\phi|\mathcal T\psi\rangle=\langle\psi|\phi\rangle$. With $\phi=\mathcal T\psi$: $\langle\mathcal T^2\psi|\mathcal T\psi\rangle=\langle\psi|\mathcal T\psi\rangle$, i.e. $-\langle\psi|\mathcal T\psi\rangle=\langle\psi|\mathcal T\psi\rangle=0$. If $[H,\mathcal T]=0$, $\mathcal T\psi$ is a second, orthogonal eigenstate of the same energy.

keyPoints: conjugation is forced by the first time derivative

source.where: Ch. 7.1-7.8 (questions in the spirit of the lecturer ch7 pack)

questions.q: Why must a symmetry act on $\mathcal H$ by unitary (or anti-unitary) operators rather than any invertible ones?
questions.explain: Measurable content is $|\langle\phi|\psi\rangle|^2$ on rays; Wigner: only unitary or anti-unitary maps preserve it.

questions.q: Which $j$ give honest representations of SO(3)?

questions.explain: Kernel of the conjugation map $\tilde x\mapsto g\tilde xg^\dagger$.

questions.q: In the cocycle condition, what forces $c(g_1,g_2)c(g_1g_2,g_3)=c(g_2,g_3)c(g_1,g_2g_3)$?
Can a genuinely projective representation of an abelian group have anticommuting operators $U(g)U(h)=-U(h)U(g)$?
options: Yes, e.g. $\mathbb Z_2\times\mathbb Z_2$ with $\sigma_3,\sigma_1$ (sheet 10 Q2)
No, abelian groups only have 1D irreducibles
questions.explain: The ratio $c(g,h)/c(h,g)=-1$ survives every re-phasing; honest irreducibles of abelian groups are 1D, projective ones need not be.

questions.q: Why do the spherical harmonics contain no half-integer $l$?
options: $e^{im\varphi}$ must be single-valued on the sphere
questions.explain: $\varphi\to\varphi+2\pi$ must give the same function, so $m\in\mathbb Z$.

options: selection rules and Kramers degeneracy, but no conserved quantity
questions.explain: Anti-unitary operators have no hermitian generator.

questions.q: The Casimir $\vec M^2$ on $\mathcal D_j$ equals
questions.explain: It commutes with all $M_k$, so by irreducibility it is a multiple of $\mathbb 1$; evaluate on the top state: $M_-M_++M_3^2+M_3=j^2+j$.
